solventWindow.title: The solvent bench
solventWindow.subtitle: Set a world's surface temperature, then ask what could still flow there — and whether a cell could be built in it
solventWindow.aria: Liquid temperature ranges for four candidate biological solvents, with {count} of them liquid at the temperature currently set
solventWindow.gateLabel: What a cell needs from its solvent
solventWindow.windowNote: How wide a climate the liquid tolerates
solventWindow.polarityNote: Higher pulls polar molecules apart more strongly
solventWindow.liquidCountNote: Candidates still flowing at this temperature

water.solvation: Every polar biomolecule you are made of goes into solution in it — sugars, salts, amino acids, the phosphate spine of DNA.
water.folding: Folding is driven by water: oily parts of a protein flee it and huddle inward while the rest embrace it, and that flight is what carves an enzyme's shape.
water.membrane: A lipid bilayer assembles itself in water for the same reason — oily tails inward, water-loving heads out. No instruction needed, only the solvent.

ammonia.solvation: Polar and cosmically abundant, so it dissolves polar compounds respectably — the reason it stays on every serious list of alternative solvents.
ammonia.folding: It hydrogen-bonds, so an ammonia version of the fold-driving effect is not excluded. Nobody has shown one working, and no molecule is known to do it.
ammonia.membrane: Ordinary bilayers are tuned to water. Whether an equivalent sheet could hold together in liquid ammonia is an open theoretical question.

methane.solvation: Non-polar, so the polar molecules biochemistry runs on barely dissolve in it at all. A different chemistry would be needed from the ground up.
methane.folding: With no hydrogen bonding there is nothing for an oily group to flee, so the effect that folds every one of your enzymes simply does not exist here.
methane.membrane: A lipid bilayer cannot form in a non-polar liquid. Theorists have to invent an entirely different membrane for Titan's seas to make cells thinkable.

formamide.solvation: More polar than water, and a better medium than water for exactly the phosphate chemistry that assembles a genetic backbone.
formamide.folding: Its polarity leaves room for a folding effect in principle, but no protein is known to fold in it and the mechanism has never been demonstrated.
formamide.membrane: No self-assembling membrane has been shown in formamide. The gap between a promising solvent and a working cell is still unbridged.

verdict.water: Water flows here, and it is the only candidate that clears all three requirements: it dissolves the molecules, it drives protein folding, and a membrane assembles in it unaided. Notice what it does not win — formamide beats it on liquid window and on polarity. That is precisely why the honest verdict is 'close to a universal optimum' rather than 'optimal'.
verdict.ammonia: Ammonia flows here, and it dissolves polar compounds well enough to stay on the list. But its liquid window at ordinary pressure is barely a quarter of water's, and neither protein folding nor a working membrane has ever been shown in it. A candidate, not a rival.
verdict.methane: Methane flows here — and that is nearly the end of the good news. Being non-polar, it dissolves almost nothing biochemistry needs, offers no folding effect, and will not hold a lipid bilayer. Life in Titan's seas would need a chemistry invented from scratch, running at a geological crawl.
verdict.formamide: Formamide flows here, and it out-scores water on both headline numbers: a liquid window twice as wide and higher polarity, plus better phosphate chemistry for assembling a genetic backbone. What it lacks is any demonstration of folding or a membrane. Keep it as the reason to say 'close to' optimal — and to keep the door open.
verdict.notLiquid: At this temperature the chosen solvent is not a liquid at all, so the question of whether a cell could be built in it does not arise. A solvent that is frozen or boiled away is no solvent. This is the first and crudest filter any living world has to pass.

networkOrMind.title: Network or mind?
networkOrMind.subtitle: Four checks in series, and five specimens to run through them — including two whose answers we already know
networkOrMind.aria: A diagnostic bench of four consecutive checks; a signal travels along it and stops at the first check the chosen specimen fails
networkOrMind.gateLabel: How this specimen answered each check

gates.competence: Solves problems it was never told about
gates.broadcast: Broadcasts one content to the whole system
gates.experience: Something it is like to be it

hint.slimeMould: One cell, no neurons, and it reproduces the Tokyo rail map. It stalls at integration: thick tubes where flow is high is a local rule, not a whole bound into something irreducible. Competence without a candidate for a mind — and the cleanest proof the first check on this bench is not the interesting one.
hint.beeSwarm: The swarm makes a genuinely good decision with no decider, and its piping signal is the closest thing here to a broadcast. But it carries a single alarm, not arbitrary content offered to every processor, and the swarm never binds into one irreducible system. Brilliant, and nobody home.
hint.cerebellum: The control that matters. Four-fifths of your neurons sit here, and people who lose it stay fully conscious. It stalls at the very first architectural check because it is a one-way pipeline. If a test cannot fail the biggest heap of connections in your skull, it is only counting parts.
hint.cortex: The other control: the one specimen that runs the whole bench. Saturated with recurrent loops, wired for the sudden system-wide ignition that makes a content conscious — and it is the sole case where the last check is answered from the inside rather than guessed from outside.
hint.eywa: Now the specimen this chapter is about. Eywa clears competence outright — the wildlife surge, the balance kept for millennia. It stalls at integration, because root-and-mycelial signalling is slow and diffuse, with dense pockets at hubs like the Tree of Souls rather than one irreducible planetary whole. Memory access is a query at one tree, not an ignition across a world. And the last check is not a low score; it is unanswerable from outside, exactly as it is for the person beside you.

slimeMould.competence: Set on food laid out like the cities around Tokyo, it floods every route, then prunes until what remains matches a rail network humans took decades to optimise.
slimeMould.recurrence: Its feedback is real but local: tubes carrying more flow thicken, the rest wither. The network never becomes a whole that cannot be carved into independent parts.
slimeMould.broadcast: Nothing here selects a content and makes it available system-wide. Every region responds to the flow in its own tubes.
slimeMould.experience: No structure of the kind either framework requires, and none of its competence needs one. The answer is a plain no.

beeSwarm.competence: Scouts dance, inspect each other's finds, and count their neighbours; the colony reliably picks the best cavity available. No bee compares all the options.
beeSwarm.recurrence: Recruitment feeds back on itself at each site, which is genuine integration — but it stays local to the candidate, never welding the swarm into one irreducible system.
beeSwarm.broadcast: The piping signal genuinely goes out to everyone and shuts down competing dances. It carries one message, though, not any content the whole colony might need.
beeSwarm.experience: Individual bees may well have inner lives. The swarm as an entity shows no sign of one, and its decision needs none.

cerebellum.competence: It runs the arithmetic of balance and fine movement continuously and superbly. Lose it and your gait, speech, and coordination fall apart.
cerebellum.recurrence: Almost purely feed-forward: signals pour in one direction, are processed, and exit. On Integrated Information Theory's own terms a feed-forward system unfolds into independent chains, so its integrated information is essentially nil.
cerebellum.broadcast: No workspace, no ignition. It reports its results onward instead of lighting up the whole brain with them.
cerebellum.experience: The decisive empirical fact on this bench: people missing a cerebellum are motorically impaired and fully conscious. Sixty-nine billion neurons, and the lights stay on without them.

cortex.competence: Perception, language, planning, and the ordinary miracle of recognising a face — the specimen every other entry here is implicitly compared against.
cortex.recurrence: Saturated with re-entrant loops and locked in constant conversation with the thalamus. Information reverberates, re-enters, and binds instead of merely passing through.
cortex.broadcast: The signature is 'ignition': a sudden system-wide flare of synchronised activity that puts one content in front of every specialised processor at once.
cortex.experience: The one case answered from the inside. You are reading this, which is not evidence available for any other specimen on the bench.

eywa.competence: Coordinates a continent-wide defence, holds a biosphere's balance for millennia, and stores whole personalities with enough fidelity to replay them. Competence is not in question anywhere in this chapter.
eywa.recurrence: Grace's connection count is real and beside the point. Root-to-root chemical and bioelectric signalling is slow and diffuse — dense local integration at hubs like the Tree of Souls, no evidence of one fast, irreducible, planet-spanning whole.
eywa.broadcast: Canon shows point-to-point access: a body plugs into one specific tree to reach one specific memory. That is a query answered off a drive, not a planet flaring into a single shared moment.
eywa.experience: Unanswerable, and saying so is the honest result rather than a hedge. Subjective experience cannot be read off behaviour from outside — not for Eywa, and not for anyone else either.

ventBattery.title: The battery in the rock
ventBattery.subtitle: Set the two fluids and the temperature, then read the voltage the pH difference alone produces
ventBattery.aria: An alkaline vent fluid and an acidic ocean separated by a thin mineral wall, currently producing {mv} millivolts of drive
ventBattery.cellBand: {min}–{max} mV: what a cell runs on
ventBattery.deltaPhNote: How far downhill a proton falls

verdict.below: At this setting the rock supplies less drive than a living cell uses. Widen the pH gap and watch how easily it catches up — the gradient is the cheap part.
verdict.cellRange: The bare rock is now delivering the same electrical drive a modern cell's ATP synthase runs on — with no pump, no membrane protein, no genome. This is the whole case for a vent origin.
verdict.above: The rock is out-driving a living cell by about {ratio}× — a geological gradient handing over more voltage than biology bothers to use. Energy was never the scarce thing.

errorThreshold.title: The ceiling on remembering
errorThreshold.subtitle: How long a sequence can a copier protect, if it makes mistakes at this rate?
errorThreshold.aria: Maximum sustainable sequence length against per-base copying fidelity, currently {length} nucleotides
errorThreshold.needNote: To fold into a working copier

verdict.shortOfReplicase: Short by about {shortfall} nucleotides. The copier cannot protect a sequence long enough to encode the copier — and nothing on any world lets you skip that step.
verdict.clearsReplicase: Now the ceiling clears the length a replicase needs. But look where the slider had to go to get here: that accuracy is what a folded replicase would provide, which is precisely what does not exist yet.

wetDryRatchet.title: The ratchet on the shore
wetDryRatchet.subtitle: Watch a pool dry and refill, and watch what survives each round
wetDryRatchet.aria: A drying and refilling rock pool building oligomers, currently reaching {n} units

hint.cycled: Drying drives the joins; refilling breaks most of them and keeps the rest. Neither phase alone builds anything — the alternation does, and each round starts from a slightly longer chain than the last.
hint.submerged: Held under water the whole time, the reaction never flips. Synthesis and breakdown balance at the shortest fragments, and the chain simply never grows. This is the price of the vent scenario: the best battery sits where nothing can polymerise.

wetDryRatchet.cyclesNote: Each one a chance to keep something

originScoreboard.title: Six things an origin has to do
originScoreboard.subtitle: Three settings proposed for where life began, graded honestly on each step — and what Pandora changes
originScoreboard.hint: Pandora improves {gains} of the six rows, and every one of them is about raw material or energy. {stuck} rows are handled well by no setting at all — and those are the ones about information.

scenario.pool: Drying pools on a volcanic shore

scenarioNote.spark: Electrical discharge through a volcanic atmosphere makes the small molecules easily — but leaves them dissolved in an ocean too dilute to build anything from.
scenarioNote.vent: Warm alkaline fluid meeting cold acidic water across mineral walls supplies free electrical drive for as long as the rock lasts. The same warmth shreds long chains.
scenarioNote.pool: Evaporation concentrates and joins; refilling selects and wraps. The strongest answer for polymers, and the most vulnerable to simply drying up for good.

detail.monomers: Amino acids, sugars, bases and fatty acids have to appear from volcanic gas and water. This is the part that is genuinely solved: they form readily under many plausible conditions, and meteorites deliver more.
detail.polymers: Joining two units expels a water molecule, so in bulk water chains fall apart as fast as they form. Something has to remove the water — drying, or a mineral surface that holds the pieces in place.
detail.information: A sequence must be copied accurately enough that what worked is still there next generation. Nobody has demonstrated a molecule that copies itself without help, and the accuracy needed to encode such a molecule is the accuracy it would provide.
detail.compartments: Without a boundary, anything useful diffuses away and no lineage can compete with another. Fatty-acid bags assemble, grow and split on their own, which makes this the least troublesome row after monomers.
detail.energy: Every step above runs uphill, so something must push continuously for as long as it takes. A pH difference across a thin mineral wall does exactly that, for free, for the lifetime of the rock.
detail.darwin: At some point a chemical system stops being chemistry that repeats and becomes a population that varies, inherits and is selected. No experiment has crossed this line, in any setting.

pandoraDetail.monomers: Pandora is richer here than early Earth ever was: hydrogen sulfide is global rather than confined to vent fields, and the atmosphere is heavy with carbon dioxide. More feedstock, everywhere, continuously.
pandoraDetail.polymers: More cycles than Earth gets. Tides from a gas giant, plus regular eclipses, give a shoreline pool many more chances per year to dry out and refill.
pandoraDetail.information: Nothing about Pandora helps. Copying accuracy is a property of the chemistry, not of the planet, and no amount of energy or feedstock buys any of it.
pandoraDetail.compartments: The same as Earth. Fatty acids self-assemble according to their own chemistry; a livelier moon neither helps nor hinders.
pandoraDetail.energy: Pandora's advantage at its largest. Tidal flexing from Polyphemus keeps the interior hot independently of the star, so serpentinising vents can run for as long as the orbit lasts rather than as long as the planet takes to cool.
pandoraDetail.darwin: Untouched. This is the row where being the most geologically alive moon in the neighbourhood earns nothing at all.
